newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government calls another confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy government calls another confidence vote.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government called another confidence test on a decree for the transport sector on Tuesday within hours of a comfortable victory in a do-or-die vote on budget measures.

Prodi won Tuesday's confidence vote, called to sweep aside opposition amendments to the final part of his 1997 austerity budget, thanks to hard-left ally Communist Refoundation but faces a tough battle convincing it to accept more budget pain.
Prodi met Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti early on Tuesday to persuade him of the need for more deficit-cutting to prepare Italy for the launch of a European single currency.

Bertinotti promised to support Tuesday's confidence motion in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), which was carried by 308 votes to 257, with one abstention, but he repeated his concerns about another round of belt-tightening.
"We consider a mini-budget to be unnecessary, and if it was up to us we would not do it," Bertinotti said.
"But the government thinks it is necessary so we are open to talks," he told reporters, adding that Refoundation could not accept any further cut in social spending or additional taxes.

Italy has adopted a series of increasingly tough budgets over the past five years in a bid to repair the damage done by free-spending administrations at the end of the 1980s and become a founder member of Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.
The latest package of measures, which was mostly approved by parliament last December, was designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($37.5 billion) off the public sector deficit in 1997.

However the final segment, which accounts for 4.3 trillion lire of savings, was only introduced as a cabinet decree. Its passage onto the statute books was threatened by a wave of amendments, forcing the government to hold the confidence vote.

Sergio Mattarella, leader of the centrist PPI party in the Chamber, told reporters after a meeting of parliamentary party leaders late on Tuesday that another confidence vote would be held on a decree covering arrangements for the transport sector.
Under a Constitutional Court ruling, governments can no longer roll over expiring decrees and Prodi has resorted to confidence votes several times, winning with ease.
Prodi had hoped that the 1997 budget would be enough to allow Italy a place at the birth of EMU, but his plans were wrecked by an unexpected surge in 1996 state spending.
To mop up the overshoot, he announced last week that his centre-left cabinet was working on a new mini-budget, which would focus on structural changes.
Analysts expect it to include up to 15 trillion lire of deficit cuts and many have urged Prodi to prune welfare spending -- especially the generous state pensions system.
News of yet more budget medicine met a frosty reception from left wingers and the biggest trades union confederation CGIL.
"A mini-budget is useless and unwelcome," Cgil leader Sergio Cofferati told La Stampa newspaper on Tuesday.
But Prodi got backing for his crusade to tame the deficit from European Union Commissioner, Mario Monti.

"Today one can say that Italy probably will take part in the single currency," Monti told a parliamentary committee in Rome. "Only a few months ago...it seemed certain that it would be excluded. Italy has taken a major step forward." ($1 = 1,666 lire)
